When you call set_content with a str that has non-ASCII text, the charset is always UTF-8 unless you
pass another one. The transfer encoding is picked by a heuristic in _encode_text. I read the code   
but didn't run it. The line numbers below come from the files in email/.                            

1. Dispatch                                                                                         

 • email/message.py:1214: EmailMessage.set_content calls super().set_content(...). Afterwards it    
   adds MIME-Version: 1.0 if it's missing (lines 1216–1217).                                        
 • email/message.py:1142-1145: MIMEPart.set_content uses self.policy.content_manager when you don't 
   pass one.                                                                                        
    • MIMEPart.__init__ (lines 991-995) defaults the policy to email.policy.default.                
    • That policy sets content_manager = raw_data_manager (email/policy.py:97).                     
 • email/contentmanager.py:31-38: ContentManager.set_content does three things.                     
    • It rejects multipart messages.                                                                
    • It finds a handler by walking the MRO of type(obj) (_find_set_handler, lines 40-59).          
    • It calls msg.clear_content() and then the handler.                                            
 • email/contentmanager.py:196: str is registered to set_text_content.                              

2. Charset                                                                                          

set_text_content is at email/contentmanager.py:185-195.                                             

 • The signature has charset='utf-8' and cte=None (line 185). So the charset is not detected from   
   the text. It is UTF-8 unless the caller says otherwise.                                          
 • Line 189 calls _encode_text(string, charset, cte, msg.policy).                                   
 • Lines 191-193 write the charset parameter, mapping it through email.charset.ALIASES.             
 • Line 194 sets Content-Transfer-Encoding to the cte that _encode_text returned.                   
 • Line 99 (_prepare_set) sets Content-Type: text/<subtype>.                                        

3. Transfer encoding: _encode_text (email/contentmanager.py:145-182)                                

The inputs are maxlen = policy.max_line_length or sys.maxsize (line 147). The default policy has    
max_line_length = 78 (_policybase.py:181) and cte_type = '8bit' (_policybase.py:180). lines =       
string.encode(charset).splitlines() (line 148) encodes the text to bytes first.                     

If cte is None, which is the default (line 152), the choice goes in this order:                     

 1 7bit (lines 154-158). If the longest line is within maxlen and the body decodes as ASCII, it     
   returns '7bit'. Non-ASCII text fails this check.                                                 
 2 8bit (lines 159-160). If all lines fit within maxlen and policy.cte_type == '8bit', it returns   
   '8bit'. The bytes are decoded with surrogateescape so the raw bytes stay in the str payload. This
   is the default policy, so short-line UTF-8 text normally ends up as 8bit.                        
 3 Quoted-printable or base64 (lines 161-170). This is reached if a line is too long, or if the     
   policy's cte_type is '7bit', as in a custom 7bit policy.                                         
    • It takes the first 10 lines as a sample (sniff, line 161).                                    
    • It encodes the sample both ways: sniff_qp with quoprimime.body_encode (line 162) and          
      sniff_base64 with binascii.b2a_base64 (line 163).                                             
    • If QP is longer than base64, it picks base64 (lines 165-166). Otherwise it picks              
      quoted-printable (line 168), and if there are 10 lines or fewer it returns the sample's QP    
      form directly (lines 169-170).                                                                

The actual encoding happens at lines 171-181:                                                       

 • 7bit or 8bit: the lines are joined with \n.                                                      
 • quoted-printable: quoprimime.body_encode(..., maxlen) runs on the latin-1 view of the bytes (line
   176). body_encode is at quoprimime.py:153. It escapes special characters and soft-wraps lines    
   with =.                                                                                          
 • base64: the code calls _encode_base64 (lines 136-142). It splits the data into chunks of         
   maxlen//4*3 bytes and encodes each chunk. The joined lines use the policy's linesep              
   (embedded_body, line 150).                                                                       
 • Explicit cte: if you pass cte= yourself, the heuristic is skipped. A cte of '7bit' with non-ASCII
   text raises, because the ASCII decode at line 172 fails. A cte that isn't one of the four known  
   values raises ValueError (line 181).                                                             

The payload is then stored with msg.set_payload(payload) (line 190).                                

4. Final bytes: the generator                                                                       

as_bytes (message.py:202-213) uses BytesGenerator, which goes through Generator._write              
(generator.py:~170-204).                                                                            

 1 Body first. The body is written into a buffer by _dispatch (lines 182-183, 206-220). For text/*  
   it calls _handle_text.                                                                           
 2 Surrogate check. BytesGenerator._handle_text (generator.py:446-456) checks the payload for       
   surrogates.                                                                                      
    • This applies to the 8bit case, where the payload holds surrogate-escaped bytes.               
    • If the policy isn't 7bit, it writes the payload straight out (lines 451-454).                 
      BytesGenerator.write (line 421) does s.encode('ascii', 'surrogateescape'), which turns the    
      surrogates back into the original UTF-8 bytes.                                                
    • Otherwise it falls to Generator._handle_text (lines 245-264).                                 
 3 7bit-policy fallback. In Generator._handle_text, if surrogates are present and a charset is      
   known, the message is deep-copied and re-encoded with set_payload(..., charset) (lines 251-259). 
   It records _munge_cte (lines 260-261), and lines 189-196 then rewrite the headers to match.      
 4 Line endings. _write_lines (generator.py:151-160) converts line endings to the policy's linesep. 
 5 Headers. After the body, _write_headers (lines 429-444) writes the headers via                   
   policy.fold_binary. Content-Type: text/plain; charset="utf-8" and Content-Transfer-Encoding: ... 
   come out as ASCII. The code writes a blank line, then the buffered body (generator.py:204).      

Summary                                                                                             

                                                                                                    
 Condition                                     Result                                               
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 
 Default policy, all lines ≤ 78 bytes          8bit, raw UTF-8 bytes                                
 Line > 78 bytes, or a cte_type='7bit' policy  quoted-printable or base64, whichever is shorter on  
                                               the first 10 lines                                   
 cte= passed                                   Used as given (no heuristic)                         
 charset= passed                               Used for .encode and the charset param. The default  
                                               is utf-8.                                            
                                                                                                    

Two caveats:                                                                                        

 • With policy.SMTP, max_line_length is still 78, but linesep is \r\n.                              
 • HTTP sets max_line_length=None, which becomes sys.maxsize, so the line-length check never        
   triggers.

2. **8bit** (lines 159-160). If all lines fit within `maxlen` and `policy.cte_type == '8bit'`, it returns `'8bit'`. The bytes are decoded with `surrogateescape` so the raw bytes stay in the str payload. This is the default policy, so **short-line UTF-8 text normally ends up as 8bit**.
